name: Testing
description: The test pyramid, doubles, TDD, property-based testing and writing tests that survive refactoring.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Testing is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is software testing, and why automate it?
cards.answer: Checking that software does what it should and keeps doing so as it changes. Automated tests are code that runs the program and checks results, so the whole suite can re-run in seconds on every change.
cards.explanation: The main value of automated tests is confidence to change code: refactoring and adding features without fear of silently breaking what already worked.

cards.prompt: What is a unit test?
cards.answer: A small, fast test that checks one piece of code — usually a function or class — in isolation: given these inputs, expect this output.
cards.explanation: Unit tests run in milliseconds, so you can have thousands and run them constantly. Each test should check one behaviour and have a name that says what it checks.

cards.prompt: What is the test pyramid?
cards.answer: A guideline for balancing test types: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle (checking components work together), and a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top (driving the whole system like a user).
cards.explanation: Higher-level tests give more realistic confidence but are slower and flakier. An "ice cream cone" suite, mostly end-to-end tests, is slow and painful to maintain.

cards.prompt: What is the Arrange–Act–Assert structure?
cards.answer: A simple shape for every test: arrange the inputs and setup, act by calling the code under test, assert that the result is what you expected.
cards.explanation: Keeping the three phases visibly separate makes tests easy to read and keeps each test focused on one behaviour.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Unit testing best practices

cards.prompt: What is a regression, and a regression test?
cards.answer: A regression is a bug in something that used to work, introduced by a later change. A regression test is written to catch it — typically reproducing a fixed bug so it can never quietly return.
cards.explanation: A good habit: when you fix a bug, first write a test that fails because of it, then fix the code so the test passes.

modules.name: Strategy & Structure
modules.description: What to test at which level, and what a good test looks like.

cards.prompt: What is the test pyramid, and what is the trade-off it encodes?
cards.answer: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a small number of end-to-end tests. Speed and determinism decrease as you go up; confidence that the whole system works increases.
cards.explanation: An inverted pyramid — mostly E2E — gives slow, flaky suites nobody trusts. All-unit gives fast green builds over a system that does not actually work. The 'testing trophy' argues for weighting integration tests most heavily, which is reasonable for typical web applications.

resources.title: Martin Fowler — The practical test pyramid

cards.prompt: Name the kinds of test double and what each is for.
cards.answer: Dummy (filler, never used), stub (returns canned answers), spy (records calls), mock (asserts on expected interactions), fake (a working lightweight implementation, such as an in-memory repository).
cards.explanation: Fakes usually age best — they exercise real behaviour without real infrastructure. Mocks that assert on every internal call couple the test to the implementation, so a refactor that changes nothing observable still breaks the suite.

cards.prompt: Why will this test break during a harmless refactor?
cards.code:
def test_checkout():
    service.checkout(cart)
    assert repo.save.call_count == 3
    assert logger.info.called
    assert mailer.send.call_args[0][0] == 'order.tpl'
cards.answer: It asserts on implementation details — how many saves, that logging happened, which template was used. Assert on observable behaviour instead: the order exists, is paid, and a confirmation was sent to the customer.
cards.explanation: A good test describes *what* the system does, so it fails only when behaviour changes. Tests coupled to internals actively discourage refactoring, which is the opposite of what they are for.

resources.title: Google Testing Blog — Test behaviour, not implementation

cards.prompt: A well-structured test follows Arrange, Act, ___.
cards.answer: Assert
cards.explanation: One logical assertion per test keeps failures diagnostic — you learn what broke from the test name alone. If a test needs several acts, it is probably several tests. Name tests after the behaviour: `rejects_expired_coupon`, not `test_checkout_2`.

modules.name: Techniques
modules.description: TDD, coverage, property-based testing and testing the awkward parts.

cards.prompt: What is the TDD cycle, and what does it actually give you?
cards.answer: Red (write a failing test), green (make it pass simply), refactor (clean up with the test as a safety net). What it buys is testable design, an executable specification, and immediate feedback — not merely coverage.
cards.explanation: Writing the test first forces you to use your own API before you build it, which surfaces awkward dependencies early. It is a design tool as much as a verification one — and it is not a religion; exploratory spikes are fine, just throw them away.

cards.prompt: Your team hits 100% line coverage. What does that guarantee?
cards.answer: That every line executed during the tests — nothing more. It says nothing about assertions being meaningful, edge cases being covered, or branch and path combinations being exercised.
cards.explanation: Coverage is a good *negative* signal: 20% coverage tells you something real. As a target it invites gaming — tests that call code and assert nothing. Branch coverage is more informative than line coverage, and mutation testing measures whether your assertions actually catch changes.

cards.prompt: What does property-based testing add over example-based tests?
cards.answer: Instead of fixed cases you state a property that must always hold — `decode(encode(x)) == x`, 'the result is always sorted' — and the framework generates hundreds of inputs, shrinking any failure to a minimal counterexample.
cards.explanation: It finds the edge cases you did not imagine: empty inputs, unicode, huge values, NaN, duplicates. Hypothesis (Python), fast-check (JS) and QuickCheck (Haskell) are the standard tools. Round-trip and invariant properties are the easiest to start with.

cards.prompt: How do you test code that depends on time, randomness or the network?
cards.answer: Inject them. Pass a clock, a random source and an HTTP client as dependencies so tests can supply deterministic versions. Use fake timers, seeded RNGs, and recorded or stubbed HTTP responses.
cards.explanation: 'This is hard to test' almost always means 'this has hidden dependencies'. Making them explicit improves the design regardless of testing. For third-party APIs, contract tests plus a recorded fixture beat either mocking blindly or hitting the real service in CI.

cards.prompt: What is the first thing to do when a bug is reported?
cards.answer: Write a failing test that reproduces it. Then fix it. The test proves the diagnosis, proves the fix, and stops the bug returning.
cards.explanation: Fixing without a reproducing test means you are guessing about both cause and cure. This habit also grows your suite where it matters most — around the code that has actually proven capable of being wrong.

modules.name: Kinds of Tests
modules.description: Integration tests with real dependencies, contract, end-to-end, snapshot, mutation, fuzzing, load and characterisation tests.

cards.prompt: Your repository tests mock the database driver and all pass, but production queries fail. What should the tests do instead?
cards.answer: Run them against a real instance of the same database engine and version — started per test run with Testcontainers or a CI service container — with the schema created by your real migrations. Isolate tests with transactions rolled back after each test, or unique data per test.
cards.explanation: Mocking a database only verifies that you called the mock the way you expected; SQL syntax, constraints, transactions and query plans go untested. SQLite standing in for Postgres misses dialect differences. Real dependencies in containers are now cheap enough to be the default.

cards.prompt: What is consumer-driven contract testing?
cards.answer: Each consumer records the requests it makes and the response fields it relies on, as a contract. The provider's CI verifies it still satisfies every consumer's contract, so a breaking change fails the provider's build before deploy — without spinning up the whole system.
cards.explanation: It replaces slow, brittle end-to-end environments for checking service compatibility. Pact is the common tool; schema-based alternatives check OpenAPI or protobuf compatibility. Contracts capture only what consumers use, so providers stay free to change everything else.

cards.prompt: What makes browser end-to-end tests reliable instead of flaky?
cards.answer: Select elements by role or accessible name (`getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`) rather than CSS paths; rely on auto-waiting assertions instead of fixed sleeps; give each test isolated data and state; mock only third parties you do not control; and keep the suite to critical user journeys.
cards.explanation: Tools such as Playwright auto-wait for elements and record traces, videos and screenshots on failure, which makes flakes diagnosable. Role-based selectors double as an accessibility check: if a test cannot find the button by its name, neither can a screen reader.

cards.prompt: Snapshot tests vs explicit assertions
cards.answer: A snapshot test serialises output (rendered markup, JSON) and compares it with a stored copy; explicit assertions check specific properties you care about.

left.title: Snapshot
points: Whole output compared to a stored file
Fast to write, catches any change

cards.explanation: Snapshots are cheap to write and catch unintended changes broadly, but large snapshots get approved without reading ("just update them"), so they stop protecting anything. Keep snapshots small and focused, or prefer assertions on what matters. They suit serialisers, CLIs and error messages.

cards.prompt: What does mutation testing measure that coverage does not?
cards.answer: It makes small deliberate changes (mutants) to your code — flip `<` to `<=`, `+` to `-`, delete a call — and reruns the tests. A mutant that no test catches reveals code that is executed but not actually verified.
cards.explanation: Coverage says code ran; mutation score says tests would notice if it were wrong. It is expensive, so run it on critical modules or on changed files. Tools: Stryker (JS/TS, .NET), PIT (Java), mutmut (Python), cargo-mutants (Rust).

resources.title: Stryker Mutator — What is mutation testing?

cards.prompt: What is fuzzing, and where does it find bugs other tests miss?
cards.answer: Automatically feeding huge numbers of generated or mutated inputs to code, guided by coverage feedback, looking for crashes, hangs, sanitizer errors or broken invariants. It excels at parsers, decoders, protocol handlers and anything consuming untrusted input.
cards.explanation: Coverage-guided fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL++, Go's built-in `go test -fuzz`, cargo-fuzz, Atheris for Python) have found thousands of security bugs, many through Google's OSS-Fuzz. Property-based testing is a close cousin focused on logic rather than crashes.

resources.title: Go — Tutorial: Getting started with fuzzing

cards.prompt: How do you find out how much traffic your service can handle before launch day?
cards.answer: Load test a production-like environment with realistic traffic shapes (mix of endpoints, think time, data volume), ramping up while watching latency percentiles and error rates, to find the knee where latency climbs. Then run a soak test for hours to catch leaks, and a spike test for sudden bursts.
cards.explanation: Measure from the client with open-model load (requests arriving at a rate regardless of responses) — closed-model tools that wait for each response hide overload (coordinated omission). k6, Gatling and Locust are common tools. The bottleneck found is often a database or a connection pool.

cards.prompt: You must change a 2,000-line legacy function with no tests and no documentation. How do you start safely?
cards.answer: Write characterisation tests first: call the code with representative inputs and assert whatever it currently returns — capturing actual behaviour, bugs included. Then refactor in small steps under that safety net, introducing seams so pieces can be tested alone.
cards.explanation: The goal is not to judge the behaviour but to notice when it changes. Approval (golden-master) testing records large outputs to make this quick. Michael Feathers' definition applies: legacy code is simply code without tests.

resources.title: Michael Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code

modules.name: Designing Good Tests
modules.description: Isolation and determinism, test data builders, Given–When–Then and BDD, and testing observable behaviour.

cards.prompt: Each test passes alone, but the suite fails when run in a different order. Why?
cards.answer: The tests share mutable state: `users` is module-level and never reset, so `test_count` depends on whether `test_create` ran first. Give each test its own fresh state (a fixture that builds it, or a reset in setup), so order never matters.
cards.explanation: Order dependence also hides in databases, caches, singletons, environment variables, the filesystem and the clock. Running tests in random order (pytest-randomly, Jest's `--randomize`) surfaces it early; parallel test runs surface it by force.

resources.title: Martin Fowler — Eradicating non-determinism in tests

cards.prompt: What is a test data builder, and what problem does it solve?
cards.answer: A helper that creates valid domain objects with sensible defaults, letting each test override only the fields it cares about: `an_order().with_status("paid").build()`. Tests then show exactly what is relevant to them.
cards.explanation: Without it, every test constructs full objects by hand, obscuring the one field that matters, and every new required field breaks hundreds of tests. Factory libraries (factory_boy, Fishery, Instancio) provide the same idea with persistence support.

cards.prompt: What is Given–When–Then, and what is behaviour-driven development for?
cards.answer: A structure for describing a behaviour as a scenario: Given some context, When an event happens, Then an outcome follows. BDD uses such scenarios, written together by developers, testers and product people, as shared examples of the required behaviour — sometimes executed directly (Cucumber, SpecFlow).
cards.explanation: The real value is the conversation that produces concrete examples before building; the tooling is optional. Given–When–Then is the same shape as Arrange–Act–Assert in plain language, and works equally well in ordinary test names.

cards.prompt: With limited time, which code most deserves tests?
cards.answer: Code where bugs are costly or likely: business rules and calculations (money, permissions, pricing), complex branching, code that has broken before, boundaries between components, and anything you are about to refactor. Test through public behaviour, not private helpers.
cards.explanation: Trivial getters, framework glue and generated code rarely repay tests. Risk-based priorities beat a coverage target. A good question for each test: "what bug would this catch?" — if there is no answer, it is probably not worth maintaining.

resources.title: Kent C. Dodds — Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.
